1:
The title carries the psalm, and Augustine of Hippo says so outright: it has fruit in its prolixity, and because the psalm is short we may make up for not tarrying over the psalm by tarrying over the title, on which every verse sung depends as a man depends on what is fixed on the front of the house before he enters. Saul, he says, bore the figure of a temporal kingdom belonging not to life but to death, and David the figure of Christ; the betrayal did the Ziphites no good and David no harm, since it showed their evil disposition and Saul still could not seize him. Keil and Delitzsch supply the history: one of the eight psalms from the time of Saul’s persecution, a Maskil like the two preceding, written after David, with six hundred men in the fortified town of Keilah, learned that its people would give him up. Adam Clarke carries it to the end: Saul on one side of the mountain and David on the other, an express arriving that the Philistines had invaded Israel, Saul turning back and David escaping to En-gedi. John Calvin draws the lesson from the circumstances: David notes them to teach us never to despair of divine help, and it gives a high idea of his indomitable faith to find him calling on God in the immediate prospect of death, when it might have seemed as credible that God could raise the dead. Matthew Henry is struck by where the betrayal happened. One would have thought that retiring into the country he would not be pursued, into a desert not discovered, and into his own country not betrayed; and yet he was. Never let a good man expect to be safe and easy till he comes to heaven.

What the name is that saves him is read three ways. John Gill and Adam Clarke take it for God himself, the name often standing for the person, so that David asks to be saved by God alone when no human means were left; John Wesley reduces it to two words, by thy own strength. John Calvin presses the emphasis: beyond the reach of human assistance, David prays to be saved by the name in contradistinction to the ordinary methods God generally uses. C.H. Spurgeon spreads it over the whole divine nature — employ all thine attributes for me, let every perfection blended in thy divine name work for me, is not thine honour pledged for my defence? Matthew Henry distinguishes the pleas neatly: David appeals to God’s strength, by which he was able to help him, and to his name, by which he was engaged to help him. Charles Ellicott glosses the second clause as asking that in God’s power justice be done him. C.H. Spurgeon makes the plea to be heard the last resort of saints: as long as God has an open ear we cannot be shut up in trouble, and other weapons may be useless, but no enemy can spike this gun.

The strangers are the one point of real division. John Gill allows they might be heathen soldiers Saul had hired, but thinks rather the Ziphites, of David’s own tribe, who used him as barbarously as heathens would have done and who, though of Israel, were strangers to any inward experience of divine things. John Wesley agrees they are called strangers in regard of their barbarous and perfidious carriage, and Adam Clarke assigns the two words, the strangers being the Ziphites and the oppressors Saul with his army. Charles Ellicott keeps the word foreign. The verse occurs again elsewhere with variations, some manuscripts even reading proud, so that we must understand foreign oppressors — though the inscription, he grants, may be defended by taking the word of Israelites who have degenerated and so deserve the name of aliens.
4:
The Behold is not decoration, and three voices explain it differently. John Gill takes it as a mark set on a wonder: to be helped in so extraordinary a manner deserves the attention of others, for the encouragement of their faith in like cases. Adam Clarke ties it to the moment: this would naturally occur to David when he saw Saul obliged to leave the pursuit and go to defend his territories, God’s providence having foreseen the danger and stirred up the Philistines to make their inroad just as Saul and his army were about to lay hands on him. C.H. Spurgeon makes it a cry of recognition — he saw enemies everywhere, and looking now on the band of his defenders he sees one whose aid is better than all the help of men, and is overwhelmed with joy at the sight of his divine champion. Little care we for the defiance of the foe, he adds, while we have the defence of God.

Who then upholds his soul divides the entry. Matthew Henry keeps the human defenders and puts God among them as the chief: there are some that uphold me, and God is one of them, he is the principal one, and none of them could help me if he did not help them — every creature being that to us, and no more, that God makes it to be. He adds the other sense too, that the Lord is he who upholds the soul and keeps a man from tiring in his work and sinking under his burdens. C.H. Spurgeon reads the same company but weighs it differently: the reigning Lord is in the camp of my defenders, a greater champion than any of the three mighties or all the valiant men who chose David for their captain, and like so many cyphers our friends stand for nothing till the Lord sets himself as a great unit in the front of them. Charles Ellicott removes the company altogether, preferring, with the Greek and the Latin, that God is a supporter of my life. Adam Clarke widens it in the opposite direction: the words may even refer to the Philistines, who had at this time made their inroad on Israel, so that God was with his own enemies, making them instruments to save the life of his servant. John Gill generalises the help past the occasion, to every saint helped at first conversion out of the horrible pit, the mire and clay of nature’s darkness, and afterwards in every affliction — help quick and present, seasonable and suitable, always sufficient.

The reward of the enemies is read as retribution, as promise, and as something milder. John Gill notes that the word for enemies means those who eyed him, watching his haunts as the Ziphites did under Saul’s direction, and turns the figure back on them: the pit they digged they would fall into themselves, and the net they spread for others their own feet would be taken in. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as wages — they worked for evil and shall have their pay, for it cannot be that malice should go unavenged. Adam Clarke makes the second clause an argument rather than a curse. Saul and his courtiers, instead of having God’s approbation, shall have his curse; and since God has promised to save David while these have purposed to destroy him, God’s truth is itself engaged in the defence, so that to save that truth and accomplish its promises he must cut them off. John Wesley makes the same word cut both ways, since by his truth God stands engaged to fulfil his threatenings as well as his promises. Charles Ellicott lowers the temperature of the whole line, offering put them to silence for cut them off, and according to thy faithfulness for in thy truth.
6:
The vowed sacrifice is a freewill offering, and the three voices press the word in different directions. John Gill takes it away from the altar entirely: not legal sacrifices, nor even the freewill offerings the law gives directions about, though the allusion is to them, but the freewill offerings of the mouth, the sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, offered not by constraint but of a ready mind; and the sacrifices of God’s people are their prayers and praises, their acts of beneficence, and the presentation of their souls and bodies in divine service. Adam Clarke hears generosity rather than willingness in it, rendering the line I will sacrifice nobly unto thee — not only with a willing mind but with a liberal hand. On the reason he takes the goodness to be the name’s own: thy name is good, descriptive of thy nature; and it is good to be employed in such a work, since whoever worships in sincerity is sure to be a gainer. Charles Ellicott keeps to the rendering and prefers a willing, or freewill, sacrifice.

Whether the deliverance has yet happened is the last question in the psalm. John Gill and Adam Clarke both read it as past. Gill takes it of the present trouble only, adding that this does not mean David had no more afterwards, since as soon as one trouble is gone, generally speaking, another comes. Clarke names the event: Saul had decamped to save his territories, David escaped to En-gedi, and God was most evidently the author of the deliverance. Charles Ellicott denies that the verse states anything as having happened at all; by a well-known Hebrew idiom it should be rendered, when he shall have delivered.

The closing clause draws the sharpest correction. Adam Clarke argues from the date of the psalm that the received English claims too much: this was not likely written after the death of Saul, so David could not say he had seen his desire on his enemies — and there is nothing in the text answering to his desire. The words might be translated simply, my eye hath seen my enemies, so near that I could plainly discover them, which is how almost all the versions understand it; I have seen them, and yet they were not permitted to approach me. Charles Ellicott lets the verb carry what Clarke strips out, rendering it hath gloated on and noting how expressively the Hebrews use seeing and looking, making the simple verb do almost what the eye itself can do — show hatred, love, triumph, defeat, wistfulness, disgust.
